text:
Here is my experience. I recently bought a RTX 4080 - non-super - founders edition from Best Buy (in Richfield MN, by their HQ) for $949.99 new (still crazy expensive! It was a late night impulse buy, I had a bit too much wine). I paired the 4080 with a 7800X3D combo deal from Microcenter, and I have to say it is pretty bad ass! A very noticeable increase performance at 3440x1440 from my old 3080 10GB and i7-11700K. Cyberpunk is really smooth now and DD2 is chugging along at much smoother clip (even in the capital, but that might be mostly the CPU upgrade). However, I probably should have stuck with my original upgrade schedule and waited for the 50 series later this year. 

My main takeaway is that the increase in performance is a boost from the high 40s at high and better settings up to 70+, and while that is not a massive increase percentage wise, it is an important increase for smoothness. 

I typically build a new rig with a top end NVidia GPU every four years - went from a GTX1080 to a RTX3080 (I waited in line at Microcenter for 4 hours one morning in November 2020 and got an Asus TUF OC for retail). When I upgrade, I pass on the old guts to one of my buddies for a heavily discounted price. I just sold my 11th gen i7, MB, 32GB ram, SSDs and 3080 for $500 to my buddy who's spilled a beer into his rig, my old 1080 rig. The dumbass was using it as a table and begged me to upgrade my rig so he could have my old one🙄

text:
This is NVidia doing its usual to try and gaslight people into thinking because it got a $200 price cut it us now "good value."

The fact is even after a $200 price cut it is still overpriced as a gen on gen replacement for the 3080 to the tune $200. At $750 - $800 it is an interesting card, not so much because inherently anyone wants to spend that much but because of what it does to the rest of the product stack.

You would then have to sell the 4070 Ti Super for no more than about $600 and the 4070 Super would be a $500 card, which makes sense because the 4070 Super is what the 4070 should have been as a replacement of the 3070.

Nvidia don't really care about how many 4080s they sell, they can always shift them for more anyway in the AI/datacentre space.

This is all about protecting the margins on their mid range cards.

Everything about the memory capacity & bus width in the range makes more sense when you understand that what we know as the 4070 was originally supposed to be the 3060 replacement.

What I am most angry about in all this is the tacit unspoken collusion  from AMD on this. They saw what NVidia were doing and realised that they will make better profits by not significantly competing with  NVidia on this over-tiering of cards and instead just did the same thing with just a slight offset due to mindshare advantage and features.

Both companies are amply demonstrating that they have no interest outside of profits for shareholders and why anyone is a fanboy/girl of either is a compete mystery and says much about how self delusional people are.

CUDA's many applications include: Improving game physics, graphics, and real-time interactions in gaming environments. Enhancing the simulation and analysis of sound waves, useful in fields like sonar and architectural acoustics. Used in the oil and gas industry for analyzing seismic data to locate oil reserves. Accelerating video encoding, decoding, editing, and transcoding tasks. Designing and testing aerodynamic models in automotive and aerospace industries. Financial Modeling: Used in risk management, option pricing models, and algorithmic trading for faster computations. Simulating astrophysical phenomena, particle physics simulations, and exploring quantum mechanics. Analyzing large genomic datasets, aligning DNA sequences, and understanding genetic structures. Enhancing the processing of medical images like MRI and CT scans, including reconstruction and analysis.  Simulating complex physical phenomena, like climate modeling, computational biology, and molecular dynamics. Training deep neural networks, running large-scale AI models, and accelerating machine learning algorithms. Employed for mining cryptocurrencies, where high computational power is needed for blockchain computations.

CUDA is popular because it really works, not luck.  ;)

text:
Consider the facts:  The die of the RTX 4080 super cost nvidia $116.00, $128.00(at $8.00/gigabyte) for the vram which they sell to AIBs probably at 100% margin at $488 for the die/vram kit....$150.00 for a cooler and $20.00 for the PCB so AIB cost for a full card is $658.00..so to be sold to consumers at a 30% margin(20% for partner sold to retailer and 10% margin for the retailer)this card should cost no more than $869.99 and everybody makes a decent profit margin.
The 7900 XTX die cost $94, 24 GB Vram cost $120.00 which amd sells as a kit at 100% margin for $428.88. Partner BOM would be $428.00 for the die/vram kit, $100 for a cooler and $20.00 for the PCB for a total BOM cost of $548.00 which is then sold to retailer at 20% margin...or $657.00..tac on 10% margin for the retailer the card should be at $722.00 for the consumer.
So both AMD and nvidia can drop the price on these cards and STILL make a 100% margin...So the RX 7900 XTX should be no more than $729.99 and the RTX 4080 Super no more than $869.99.

text:
When it comes to the release of the 40 series cards, I think Nvidia was trying to use Cuda Cores, Memory BUS, and Vram count to split their cards into categories, but it's like they were trying to enforce these categorizations, which is where problems came.

In terms of gaming we can split the 40 series cards into 3 categories.

A category that its specs will be suited for gaming at 1080p, and Nvidia was like:

You wanna play comfortably at 1080? Here's the 4060 for you
Wanna have more performance while playing at 1080? Here are the 4060 ti's

A category that its specs will be suited for gaming at 1440p, and Nvidia was like:

You wanna play comfortably at 1440? Here's the 4070 for you
Wanna have more performance while playing at 1440? Here's the 4070 ti

Lastly, the category that doesn't seem to have any obvious restraints on their specs, but they cost +$1000, and Nvidia was like:

Wanna see a glimpse of what it's like to do whatever you want with your card? Here's the 4080 for you
Wanna see what it's really like to do whatever you want with your card? Here's the 4090

However, I think Nvidia's plan either didn't work as intended, or it was a calculated risk anyways, or maybe both.

AMD's cards categorizations and pricing is the main reason why

For the Most part, the specs of AMD's cards at each price category makes them generally a better value than their Nvidia's counterparts.

I mean if we looked at cards like the 7700XT, 7800XT, 7900XT, and the 7900XTX, all of those cards are packed with specs and priced in a way that makes each one of them generally a better value than their Nvidia's counterparts. I mean the 7700XT's price and performance makes it a better value card than the 4060 ti's, same for the 7800XT when compared to the 4070, same for the 7900XT when compared to the 4070 ti, and same for the 7900XTX when compared to the 4080.

So unless you're someone who prefers Nvidia's cards for the things they do better than AMD's cards, and you were to purchase a graphics card from $400 to $1000 you would go for any of AMD's cards instead of Nvidia's.

This is why Nvidia's super cards came to existence, to balance things up.

The 4070 Super is faster than the 7800XT.
The 4070 ti Super is yeah still kind of behind the 7900XT but no one will be complaining about its Memory bus or Vram now.
And the 4080 Super is priced more closely to the 7900XTX and performs slightly better than its predecessor.

And it's likely that we will see a 4060 Super or a 4060 ti Super to compete with the 7600XT or the 7700XT.

text:
@4566Iggy  Marketing is messing with your head. Nvidia moved the Titan class to the 90 class because gamers were ignoring their existence. But these high end products have been on the market for a very long time. I paid $1000 for my HD 7990 in 2013. and Nvidia's (slightly slower) GTX Titan was the same price. But AMD's dual-GPU cards, and Nvidia's Titan cards were practically never mentioned, or even compared to, in GPU reviews. So gamers got used to $500-700 being the price ceiling for "gamer products" for almost two decades straight. Despite the Pascal Titan being $1500, and the Turing Titan being $2500.

Now common folk gamers have to wrap their head around the fact that the top shelf product are often outside their financial reach. Which is actually a good thing, if you ask me, because it raises the question: "If you don't habitually buy the best card available... how much performance do you actually NEED?". 

Once you have the answer to that, the mental barrier to buying a graphics card, regardless of its magic-number-moniker, that actually fits your needs, become so much easier.

Car enthusiasts do this all the time. Nobody can afford a $3.2 million Koenigsegg, so once they accept that, a Mazda MX5 suddenly looks like a car you can have a lot of fun with in your price class.

text: @user-ds8rj2vc4v There were 2 mining booms though. One happened around 2017-2018 and then another happened from late 2020 to 2022 which is the one that effected GPU pricing after GTX 3000 and RX 6000 launched on top of supply issues during the pandemic. I wasn't paying attention to mining and PCs during the first boom but I built my first PC during the pandemic in summer 2020 when GPUs were still unaffected but PSUs were in short supply. My GTX 1660 Super could be had for a discount when I bought it but the price shot up in 2021 when Ethereum was profitable and could be mined with GPUs (Dogecoin also went crazy that year from like 3 cents to around 80 cents until it crashed the day Elon Musk was on SNL). Ethereum finally went to proof-of-stake in fall 2022 (close to the launch of the 4090) which meant people couldn't mine it with GPUs anymore, so used mining GPUs flooded the market and prices started going back to normal. At $1000, the 4080 Super seems about right for a top of the line premium product in this market.  But it's the not top of the line, that's the still amazingly overpriced 4090.  The 4070 was in an OK spot for a while, and the 4070 Super is in a good spot now.  Maybe slightly overpriced, but but cards are sticking around the MSRP so far and the value of a 4070 Super makes it sit in a good spot in a bad market.  

What I'm actually curious about, and I know that's difficult to dive into without multiple samples, is how does the 4080 Super overclock vs the 4080 normal.  Given they're keeping the whole die, it's quite possible overclocking could be limited, and it could be possible to overclock a 4080 to outperform overclocked 4080 supers.  That said, given the 4080 pricing hasn't dropped, it's still a dumb investment at a cost per frame, so if you're worried about that and willing to spend $200 more for that 1-3% gap, you're buying a 4090 anyway.

I have the money to get these cards; I've been saving up for 3 years. But honestly, this is just (predictably) disappointing.
One comparison I haven't seen you make is power consumption. The 4080S is rated for 320W, whereas the 7900 XTX (default configuration) is rated for 355W (+10%), with some AIB's going over 400W.
So taking into consideration the power costs over time, the 4080S might actually be cheaper, even if bought at a premium. That being said, correcting for inflation, the 4080 is still 78% more expensive than the GTX 1080 I got in 2018 (€550 (incl. VAT)); MSRP for the 4080 will be €1210 incl. VAT. Given the price fluctuations over the past few months of high-end cards (or rather: sore lack thereof), the question is now honestly if I want to bite this bullet or just switch over to console gaming...

text:
​ @zodwraith5745  I get your point and somewhat agree, but anyone with a high refresh rate screen will generally end up not using RT in most cases even for a 4090.

Here's why:
DLDSR exists and it's a fantastic technology giving me a greater visual impact than RT 90-99% of the time when I have more performance headroom.
RT wrecks CPU performance especially 1% lows hindering the high refresh rate experience.
RT hits FPS hard pulling you out of the high refresh rate window.
DLSS simply does NOT fully negate the performance impact of RT.
RT doesn't always look great with inconsistent artifacts, one example is road reflections in Cyberpunk, SSR's reflections on the road generally looks significantly better than RT which turns the road into glass for the most part, while looking superb for other stuff.

Most of my points could be seen as subjective, but for me we only have the hardware technology to do 2 out of 3 things at the same time and for me RT is the one I would still sacrifice, if I have to choose between RT+4kDLSS, 4kDLSS+100-180FPS or RT+1080p/1440pDLSS+100-180FPS I will always choose 4kDLSS+100-180FPS.

I almost bought the 4090 since it's soo close to doing all 3 (RT+HighRes+HighRefresh) at the same time, but it just barely falls short so I will wait for next gen AMD/Nvidia GPU's and then make my choice or wait for the 4090 to become much more affordable.

I really want to go with AMD for my next GPU so here is to AMD releasing a killer flagship GPU next time round like with their 6000 series RDNA 2 GPU's.
